common_name: Jester Ornamental Pepper (Multicolor Upright Fruit Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Jester is a compact ornamental pepper bred for a heavy, colorful fruit display rather than culinary use, and does well in containers.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Jester is compact enough for containers and makes a colorful patio or border accent. It produces an abundance of small, upright, conical fruits that ripen through purple, cream, orange, and red, often showing several colors at once on a single densely branched, mounded plant covered almost entirely in fruit rather than foliage by late summer. Grown primarily for ornamental impact rather than flavor, though the small fruits are technically edible and quite hot; its dense, compact habit and heavy fruit set make it a strong seasonal color plant for beds, borders, and mixed containers through fall.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute reference

common_name: Sangria Ornamental Pepper (Deep Purple-to-Red Fruit Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Sangria is a compact ornamental pepper bred for fruit color display and does well in containers.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Sangria is compact enough for containers and makes a colorful seasonal accent for patios and borders. Its small, upright, tapered fruits ripen from deep purple-black through wine-red, giving the plant a rich, saturated color palette named for the sangria drink, held densely above dark green foliage on a tidy, mounded plant. Grown primarily for ornamental fruit display through summer and fall rather than culinary use, though the fruit is technically edible and carries significant heat; its compact size and heavy, colorful fruit set suit mixed containers, border edges, and fall seasonal plantings.

common_name: Shoo Fly Plant (Apple of Peru, Lantern-Pod Nicandra)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; self-seeds readily, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted the following year.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Shoo Fly Plant is a tall, bushy South American annual bearing pale lavender-blue, bell-shaped flowers with a white-and-purple throat through summer, followed by papery, inflated, lantern-like seed pods that resemble those of Chinese lantern (Physalis) and are popular in dried arrangements. Its old common name comes from a folk belief that the plant's foliage repels houseflies when hung or grown near a doorway, though this has not been scientifically confirmed. It self-seeds readily and can naturalize in a bed once established, so deadhead spent flowers before pods mature if volunteer seedlings are unwanted; all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, as with many nightshade-family relatives.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; the tiny seed germinates readily in warm soil but seedlings need weeding until established, since young plants are slow to compete with weeds.

directions: Surface sow or barely cover the tiny seed, then thin to 18–24 inches apart once seedlings are a couple of inches tall, in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Love-Lies-Bleeding produces long, tassel-like, drooping flower clusters in deep crimson-red that cascade a foot or more from the top of the plant, a dramatic, romantic bloom form that has made it a cottage-garden and cut-and-dried-flower favorite for centuries. The rich color and pendulous form work well as a bold vertical accent in a mixed border or cutting garden, and the flower clusters hold their color well when hung to dry for winter arrangements. It tolerates heat and drought once established and self-seeds readily, so deadhead spent flower heads before they shed seed if volunteers are unwanted the following season.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills or rows; Sharlyn is a hybrid type combining honeydew and cantaloupe parentage and needs a long, warm growing season to fully sweeten.

directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart or in rows 6 feet apart, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sharlyn is a hybrid melon combining traits of honeydew and cantaloupe, with smooth, pale ribbed skin like a honeydew but sweet, aromatic, pale orange flesh with the rich flavor of a cantaloupe, giving it an unusual combination of exterior and interior appearance that often surprises gardeners who haven't grown it before. Unlike true cantaloupe, ripe fruit does not slip easily from the vine, so judge ripeness by a color shift toward pale cream-yellow and a sweet fragrance at the blossom end rather than by fruit separation. It stores somewhat better after harvest than standard cantaloupe, making it a good choice for gardeners wanting a melon that holds a bit longer at peak quality.
